# Prologue: The Color of a Warning

The first warning came from the Dragon Dagger.

Tommy Oliver was standing alone in the desert, sixty miles outside Angel Grove, when the weapon began to sing. Not the familiar five-note call that had once brought a mechanical dragon up out of the ocean. This was lower, closer to the sound a telephone made when somebody left the line open after the conversation had ended.

The sand around his boots turned green.

"That," he told the empty landscape, "is new."

He had learned to distrust new things. Evil empresses, hidden dimensions, teenagers with talking watches: they all arrived disguised as surprises, and every surprise eventually landed him in the dirt. But this was his own weapon, the old dagger that had rested in his hand through more lives than he had any reasonable right to possess. He knew its weight. He knew the tiny shift in its balance before a bolt discharged from the dragon-shaped hilt. He knew the difference between the Grid speaking through the blade and somebody trying to make it scream.

Somebody was trying to make it scream.

Tommy drew the Sword of Darkness.

It materialized out of a folding green shadow, the blade slick with a light that did not belong in sunlight. He had once been controlled through that sword. He had broken the control years ago. The sword remained a reminder that a weapon could be turned toward a better purpose without its history being erased.

The sky split horizontally.

Not like lightning. Like a cut in film, a white seam opening across a blue afternoon. Through it he saw a city of pointed rooftops, enormous bridges, and a single black tower with the letters W and E shining above the rain.

Gotham, although he did not yet know its name.

A second seam opened behind the first, and an armored figure stepped out.

Green. White. Gold. A dragon's head reduced to a hard, elegant threat.

"Hello, Tommy," the stranger said.

Tommy kept the Sword of Darkness low. "You got a name?"

"You know it."

The voice was his own, aged by contempt.

He had seen monsters wearing his face before. He had seen a version of himself that believed authority made cruelty acceptable. The universe had an endless appetite for making Tommy Oliver confront Tommy Oliver, and very little interest in asking whether he had other plans for the day.

"Drakkon."

"You look tired."

"You look like you stole my wardrobe from a cathedral."

Drakkon tilted his head. There was no smile visible beneath the helmet, but Tommy felt one anyway.

"I have come for an inventor," Drakkon said. "A man who builds answers to questions he is afraid to ask. A man who sees a god and immediately begins designing a way to stop him."

Tommy glanced at the city in the wound. "Sounds like a fun dinner guest."

"He has already written half my victory for me."

The Dragon Dagger jumped in Tommy's fist. He fired. A green lance crossed the sand, hot enough to turn the surface to glass. Drakkon caught the beam against a palm and divided it into six bright streams that carved trenches to either side of him.

Tommy moved before the last one hit the ground.

The upgraded armor answered his intention in a way the original Green Ranger suit never had. Plates flashed into place, layered at the shoulders, forearms, and chest. The gold dragon shield became a living arrangement of overlapping scales. Everything tightened around him without restricting his breath. This was not a costume he wore. It was a transformation that understood momentum.

He struck with the Sword of Darkness.

Drakkon met it with a blade of white fire. The impact sounded like two church bells dropped down a well.

For nine seconds, the desert belonged to both of them. Tommy drove forward, cut high, stepped through a counterstrike, and fired the Dragon Dagger from under his left arm. Drakkon evaded the beam and answered with a blow that would have scattered a car into components. Tommy's armor drank part of the impact and threw the rest across the sand in a rippling ring.

Nine seconds were enough to learn something terrible.

Drakkon was not trying to win.

He was trying to move him.

The tenth strike landed against Tommy's sword and launched him backward into the open seam.

The desert vanished. Rain struck his visor. Below him sprawled a city that had never heard of Angel Grove.

Through the closing wound he heard Drakkon's voice.

"Tell him I admire his work."

Tommy fell toward Gotham.

He had survived monsters, alien wars, and a number of spectacularly bad leadership decisions. He had never fallen into a completely unfamiliar universe with an evil version of himself in pursuit.

"Okay," he said, and pointed the Dragon Dagger toward the approaching rooftop. "Today is going to suck."

The dagger fired.

The beam struck a gargoyle. The recoil threw him sideways, just enough to miss the rooftop's iron spikes. He hit a clock tower, slid down wet copper, smashed through the glass face, and landed in a room full of gears that immediately began trying to eat him.

He got up slowly.

The clock was not working anymore.

A black shape watched him from the opposite roof. Broad shoulders. Long ears. No cape movement despite the wind.

Tommy looked at it. The shape looked back.

"Let me guess," Tommy said. "You're the welcoming committee."

A voice emerged from the rain, gravel over steel.

"Put the sword down."

Tommy considered the sword, then the gargoyle, then the six-story drop between them.

"This city has terrible hospitality."

# Chapter One: The Man Who Prepared for Gods

Bruce Wayne had three minutes of footage from the clock tower and seventeen minutes of questions that the footage refused to answer.

On the Batcave's central screen, a green figure fell out of a hole in the sky, fired a weapon that appeared to violate conservation of momentum, and survived a collision with a clock tower at a velocity that should have converted his spine into a cautionary diagram.

Bruce watched the sequence again.

"Alfred."

"Yes, sir."

"The beam."

"Still green, sir."

"The recoil."

"Still impressive."

"He redirected his descent by firing it."

"And ruined an eighty-year-old clock. The preservation society will be inconsolable."

Bruce rewound to frame 218. The newcomer had not been launched upward in direct opposition to the weapon's discharge. Instead, he had adjusted course at an angle that changed throughout the burst. A normal projectile had reaction force. This behaved like an agreement between the weapon and gravity, renegotiated in real time.

"He's still alive," Bruce said.

"A considerable advantage for anyone falling through a roof."

Bruce did not smile. Alfred made a private note of the fact that, given the season, this constituted progress.

A second screen displayed the wounded clock tower. The police had cordoned off two blocks; the city's utility department was already blaming equipment failure. They did not know what equipment might cause the upper atmosphere to open like a curtain, but they were prepared to blame it anyway.

On the third screen, Bruce had pulled every word captured by the rooftop microphone.

*Put the sword down.*

*This city has terrible hospitality.*

That had been the extent of the conversation before the stranger vanished in a flash of green light. Batman had watched a man leap off an eight-story building and land on a fire escape with no visible slowing mechanism. Then the man had run along the ironwork, drawing a line of sparks with the weapon on his hip, and disappeared into Gotham's underground railway system.

There had been something in the man's stance: the relaxed ready position of somebody who knew exactly how much damage he could do, and had decided not to do it.

Bruce understood that position. He no longer trusted it.

"Trace the energy signature," he said.

Alfred set a silver tray on the workbench. "I might make the presumptuous suggestion that you first eat something."

"Later."

"You said that yesterday."

"It was true yesterday."

"Yes. And I see it has aged beautifully."

Bruce lifted his cowl. His face had the tired, compressed look of a man who had spent too many years mistaking endurance for healing. He took the coffee. The sandwich remained untouched.

"Where did it come from?" he asked.

"The clock tower?"

"The energy."

"The same place, I suspect, as that gentleman's striking sense of color. Somewhere else."

Bruce rubbed a thumb over the edge of his workstation. The suit, hanging beyond the circle of monitors, looked like a machine constructed around a bruise. The metal on its knuckles was fresh; the leather at the shoulders was older than it should have been. Twenty years of repairs. Twenty years of improving the equipment and not knowing what to do with the man wearing it.

He had once built a weapon for a visitor from the sky. He had learned, at enormous cost, that the ability to plan for an enemy did not mean he understood the person behind the power.

He had promised himself he would remember.

Now a new man had fallen through a hole in the world, armored like a dragon, holding a black sword.

Bruce opened a blank file.

ALTERNATE-REALITY ENERGY EVENT.

SUBJECT: UNKNOWN.

CAPABILITIES: UNKNOWN.

INTENT: UNKNOWN.

He stared at the cursor after the third line.

The old Bruce would have started with vulnerabilities. Materials. Heat tolerance. Maximum force. Ways to disable. Ways to kill if necessary. He had been very good at finding weaknesses, even when the weakness belonged to the person he should have trusted.

He added a fourth line.

FIRST CONTACT: ATTEMPT CONVERSATION.

Alfred, reading over his shoulder, said nothing for a long moment.

"You could frame that," he observed.

An alarm sounded from the north channel.

Six city cameras showed the same impossible thing. Traffic lights turning green in unison. Police radios broadcasting a tone too low for most listeners to notice. Subway maps briefly displaying stations from a city that did not exist. In the harbor, a tugboat captain reported a dragon's shadow moving under the water, though the depth instruments showed nothing beneath him at all.

Bruce listened to the tone through a spectral analyzer.

It contained voices.

Not words, yet. Voices folded into mathematics. Thousands of them, each slightly different, rising and falling around a common frequency.

"The suit," he said. "It's resonating with the city."

"Deliberately?"

"I don't know."

He disliked admitting it. More than that, he disliked how much relief he felt when he did.

He stood, lifted the cowl, and crossed to the armored mannequin.

Alfred took the untouched sandwich away.

"There are other people in the world, Master Bruce," he said quietly. "You might consider asking one of them for help before your latest visitor rearranges our transportation infrastructure."

Bruce sealed the cowl around his face.

"I'm going to ask him."

"With your hands?"

"If he gives me no choice."

"A remarkably elastic concept in this household."

Bruce stopped at the stairs to the Batmobile.

"Alfred."

"Yes, sir?"

"If I don't come back, shut the cave down. All of it. The files, the systems, the prototypes."

Alfred looked at the endless black stone, the banks of computers, and the broken objects of a life that had always found a way to continue.

"No," he said.

Bruce turned.

"You have spent half your life preparing for the day you might die," Alfred said. "For once, I should like to see you prepare for the possibility that you won't."

For a moment Bruce looked as though he might answer with something honest.

Then the alarm changed pitch.

The voice buried in the signal became intelligible. Not all of it, only three words, spoken by somebody who sounded strangely like the Green Ranger.

"Bring me Wayne."

The Batmobile's engine woke beneath the mountain.

"New plan," Bruce said.

Alfred sighed. "How encouraging."

# Chapter Two: A Dragon Below Gotham

Gotham's subway smelled of wet concrete, hot metal, and promises the city had never intended to keep.

Tommy stood on an abandoned platform between two rusted tracks and listened to the hum coming from the tunnel walls. Every fourth pulse, the lights flickered green. Every sixth, a voice spoke from inside the wires.

His own voice.

*Bring me Wayne.*

"Yeah," Tommy said. "Get in line."

He had found a sign in the clock tower naming the city. Gotham. The name meant nothing to him. Its architecture meant something else: a population that had spent a century preparing for the worst and then been disappointed when the worst was insufficiently imaginative.

The tunnel behind him breathed.

Tommy turned. His visor displayed an empty platform, eleven dormant cameras, and one human heartbeat approaching through the shadows above the tracks. An ordinary heartbeat. Slow. Deliberate. Trying very hard not to sound interested.

"I know you're there," Tommy said.

The dark shape detached from a maintenance gantry, cape falling around him like a broken wing.

Batman landed ten feet away.

"Good," he said.

Tommy examined the armor. Tactical plates, reinforced joints, a utility belt that might have contained anything from handcuffs to a miniature satellite. He also noted the way Batman held his left shoulder half a degree lower than his right. Old injury, chronic compensation, still functional. A fighter who had spent a lifetime paying the bills his body sent him.

"You always sneak up on people in tunnels?"

"You always fall out of the sky?"

"Not on purpose."

Batman took one step closer. "Who sent you?"

"Nobody you know."

"Try me."

"Lord Drakkon."

A tiny motion in Batman's cowl. Not surprise; filing.

"Where is he?"

"If I knew, I wouldn't be standing around in a sewer with a guy dressed like a haunted tax audit."

Batman did not respond. Tommy was starting to suspect that the man had paid good money to have his sense of humor removed.

A tremor rolled under the platform. The overhead lights turned crimson. On the opposite wall, a maintenance diagram rearranged itself into a map of Angel Grove. Tommy saw the address of his first dojo. Underneath it, the words appeared:

*YOU LEFT THEM.*

He stiffened.

Batman saw it. "What does it mean?"

"Nothing I want to discuss with a stranger."

A train horn sounded from a dead tunnel. The sound was wrong. Too large, too near, and accompanied by the scraping of metal against dimensions that had never agreed to touch.

Batman touched his cowl. "Alfred, shut down all inbound traffic to this station."

The voice in his ear answered before Alfred could.

*Too late, Bruce.*

Tommy's head snapped toward him. "You heard that?"

The third rail ignited green. A commuter train materialized half out of the tunnel wall, its windows crowded with faces, its front carriage embedded in solid masonry. People screamed. The train was real enough to carry passengers and not real enough to obey the geometry of the subway.

Batman moved first.

He fired a grapnel at the upper carriage, pulled himself across the tracks, and punched a cutting charge against the door seam. The explosion was narrow, controlled; the door came loose in his hands. He began moving passengers onto the platform, one after another, without wasting words.

Tommy watched the train's front wheel rotate through the wall as though it were smoke. Something beyond the wall was pulling it farther in.

"That thing's going to fold," he shouted.

"Then stop it," Batman answered.

Tommy almost laughed. He liked that better than another question.

He drew the Dragon Dagger and fired into the tunnel roof. The green beam forked along the steel supports and wrapped the forward carriage in a halo of light. It was not how the weapon was meant to work, and Tommy felt the strain immediately, a hot pressure behind his teeth. The Grid recognized a request to protect people. It did not understand why the request included a subway system from another universe.

He had to make it understand.

He planted the Sword of Darkness between the tracks, put his other hand against its hilt, and fed the energy through the blade.

The overhead lights went out.

For a second there was only the glow of the sword, the scream of steel, and Batman carrying a child across a gap that should not have existed.

Then the train snapped into the tunnel with an enormous metallic crack. Its wheels hit the rails. The force threw Tommy backward, shattered every clock on the station wall, and tore the cape from Batman's grip.

The last two passengers fell from the open doorway.

Batman caught one. Tommy caught the other.

The platform settled. The train remained in one piece. A little boy buried his face against Batman's armor and refused to let go.

Tommy held an older woman whose hand shook violently around his wrist.

"You all right, ma'am?"

She nodded. "What are you?"

Tommy looked down at his green armor.

"That's a long story."

She touched the gold shield on his chest. "It's a nice color."

"Thank you. I picked it myself."

Batman was already scanning the roof. His jaw was set.

"The energy was coming through the tracks," he said.

"No," Tommy answered. "It was coming through the people. The tracks just gave it somewhere to go."

Batman turned toward him.

"Explain."

"You ever get a song stuck in your head and the whole damn room seems to hum along? It's like that, but the song knows your name."

Batman glanced at the woman, the boy, the commuters moving toward the stairs. His cowl was recording them. Not just their faces. Their breathing, pulse, the microsecond gaps in the artificial frequency.

"It's using their nervous systems," he said.

"And your city is full of them."

The voice in the wall laughed softly.

*Very good, Bruce.*

The Sword of Darkness pulsed once, as though something on the other side of the universe had placed its ear against the metal.

Batman drew a compact explosive from his belt and pressed it against a conduit.

Tommy caught his wrist.

"Don't. You're about to blow the only thing keeping the passengers anchored."

For one dangerous second, the two men held perfectly still.

Batman looked down at the gauntlet gripping his wrist. Tommy felt the calibrated tension in Bruce's arm. A joint lock was being evaluated. A counterstrike. Three disabling possibilities. He could feel the calculations happening.

"You want to save them?" Tommy asked. "Listen."

Batman looked him in the visor.

Then he put the explosive away.

The green glow in the rails faded.

"I have a lab," Batman said.

"I bet you do."

"I need to understand your energy source."

"And I need to find Drakkon."

"Then we have a common problem."

Tommy looked at the ruined station, the shaken passengers, the wet black cape hanging off the man's shoulders.

"You always make friends by interrogating them?"

"Only the ones with swords."

"Fair enough. Lead on, Dracula."

Batman turned for the service stairs. Behind the cowl, Bruce Wayne nearly smiled.

# Chapter Three: The Rules of an Impossible Machine

The Batcave was a cathedral built by a man who had stopped believing that prayers were enough.

Tommy had visited alien command centers, ancient temples, secret military installations, and one spaceship shaped like a municipal building. None of them had combined computers, a medical suite, a private aircraft, and a suspended dinosaur with quite this level of sincere commitment.

"You live here?" he asked.

"No," Batman answered.

"Good. I was going to say."

An older Englishman approached carrying a tray of tea, as though two heavily armored strangers entering a cave underneath a mansion were simply a mildly inconvenient dinner-party development.

"Master Bruce," he said, "I take it your guest will be staying for supper?"

"He has a name," Batman said.

"Tommy Oliver," Tommy supplied, lifting his helmet.

Alfred looked at him, then at the strange armor, and offered a small, solemn nod.

"Alfred Pennyworth. Welcome. Should you require a towel, a shower, or the contact information for a reputable tailor, I can arrange all three."

"Coffee?"

"Now we're making progress."

Bruce removed his cowl. Tommy recognized the face immediately. Not from this universe, but from the kind of headlines that existed in every universe. Rich man. Famous man. Man whose money had become a mythology before anybody asked what he was doing with it.

"Bruce Wayne."

"Yes."

"You own this place."

"Some of it."

Tommy gazed around the enormous cave. "How much?"

"Most of it."

Alfred passed Tommy a mug. "He means all of it."

Bruce motioned toward a circular platform. "The armor. I need a scan."

Tommy set down his coffee. "You could try asking."

Bruce waited one beat. "May I scan your armor?"

"There we go."

He stepped onto the platform. Machines circled him. Each instrument registered contradictory readings. The armor reflected particles without absorbing them. It weighed thirty-eight pounds by the floor sensors, ninety-three by displacement analysis, and less than zero in one impossible magnetic measurement.

"Your instruments are broken," Tommy said.

"They're calibrated."

"Then your universe is broken."

A narrow projector scanned the Dragon Dagger. Green lines leapt across the glass in front of Bruce. He studied them with the same concentration he had once given an alien ship and an adversary's heartbeat.

"There is a pattern," he said. "Not random. It repeats, but not at fixed intervals. It adjusts to your pulse."

"The Morphin Grid."

"Explain the term."

Tommy took the mug Alfred returned to him. He had given this explanation to teenagers, generals, scientists, and one deeply skeptical talking dog. Each time it became slightly harder.

"It's energy. But calling it energy is like calling an ocean wet. It connects things. People. Worlds. Sometimes it gives a person the tools to protect other people. Sometimes somebody tries to take those tools and use them to own everybody."

Bruce's eyes stayed on the display. "A distributed network."

"Sort of."

"A field?"

"Closer."

"Does it have a central processor?"

"Buddy, if you can find one, I'd like to meet it."

Bruce expanded the image. Every line branched into another, and each branch reacted when Tommy moved his hand. When Alfred said Tommy's name, the color shifted slightly. When Bruce called up footage from the subway rescue, the diagram brightened, displaying a pattern that none of the computers had detected before.

"It responds to intention," Bruce whispered.

Tommy watched him. "Sometimes."

"Then it can be trained."

"That," Tommy said, "is a dangerous sentence."

Bruce looked up.

"There's a difference between a friend who helps you and a dog you've taught to sit. The Grid isn't your dog."

The monitors dimmed. Somewhere above them, thunder rolled across Gotham.

Bruce set the scan to read-only mode.

"What's the sword?"

Tommy's expression changed. He held the Sword of Darkness across both palms, its black edge drinking the light around it.

"A mistake I didn't get to make myself. Somebody put it in my hands when I was being controlled. Used it to keep me that way. My friends broke the spell. The sword didn't disappear from my life."

"Why carry it?"

"Because it's mine now. And if it can keep a kid from getting hurt, I'm not letting its history decide what it's good for."

Bruce knew something about objects that survived their worst owners.

He brought up the subway recording. The moment Tommy saved the train, the Grid's waveform separated into two visible strands. One belonged to Tommy. The other had been hidden behind it, almost identical, but slightly out of phase.

"Two transmitters," Bruce said.

"Two Tommys," Tommy corrected.

Bruce enlarged the second strand. It formed a line of branching possibilities: positions, strike angles, rescue routes. The kind of predictions Bruce had spent years making about people who could hurt him or people he loved.

"He's mapping us," Bruce said.

"He's mapping you," Tommy answered. "I was the bait."

The cave speakers clicked. A voice rolled over them, gentle and familiar to Tommy, vicious in its patience.

"Good evening, Mr. Wayne."

Bruce moved to sever the network connection. Tommy raised a hand.

"It isn't coming through your internet."

"You keep such interesting records," Drakkon said. "Every contingency. Every potential ally reduced to an index of weaknesses. Every problem given an answer that begins with force."

Bruce froze.

On the central screen appeared a document he had never opened during Tommy's visit.

A contingency file from a war he had nearly caused. Names. Probabilities. Modes of failure. It had been locked away beneath seventeen layers of encryption.

"How did you get that?" Bruce asked.

"You built it into yourself," Drakkon replied. "I merely listened."

The screen switched to an empty line.

It typed a question.

*HOW MANY PEOPLE WOULD YOU HURT TO KEEP GOTHAM SAFE?*

Alfred stepped forward and reached for the control panel.

# Chapter Six: The Shape of a Contingency

Bruce's first successful model of the Morphin Grid lasted seven minutes before it caught fire.

He watched the containment cylinder crack under a pressure that his instruments insisted did not exist, then shut the power down before the stored field could reach the surrounding equipment.

The cylinder collapsed inward. It did not explode. It became, in an instant, a thing that had never been built.

"I needed a baseline."

"I didn't trap it," he said.

"You built a cage. Then you were surprised when it didn't want to be in a cage."

"The analogy doesn't map."

"I think it maps fine."

*HE NEEDS YOUR PLANS. HE DOES NOT HAVE THE FINAL PIECE. DO NOT GIVE HIM THE RULES.*

Bruce read it twice.

"He's looking for the system architecture," he said.

"What architecture?" Tommy asked.

Bruce hesitated. Across the cave, old files sat in cold storage. Each one was evidence of a time he had taken a person he might love and reduced them to a problem he could solve. Strengths. "I built plans for stopping people with extraordinary abilities," he said.

"Like me?"

"Yes."

"And Drakkon thinks they're useful?"

"He thinks the methods are useful. A way to identify the thing a power source depends on, find the point of failure, and force it to comply."

"That would work on a machine," Tommy said.

"It's worked on people."

The words stayed between them.

Tommy thought of the Sword of Darkness. Of a spell wrapped around his mind so tightly that his choices had become somebody else's orders. He remembered the worst part: after the spell broke, he could still remember wanting to obey.

"I know what that's like," he said.

Bruce turned away. "I'm not asking you to trust me."

For the first time Bruce let out a breath that was almost laughter.

"Yes."

"That's not just an engineering problem," Tommy said. "How does the machine know somebody means it?"

"Maybe it doesn't," he admitted. "Maybe the Grid does."

"I suppose it is."

"Then perhaps there's hope."

Bruce looked at the dagger, then at Tommy.

"Will you help me test it?"

Drakkon regarded the circles.

There were photographs, of course. Grainy images from phones, infrared footage from harbor cameras, a shaky livestream showing an enormous shape rising out of the water and standing against the dawn. Six months later, the replacement clock at Gotham's old tower struck midnight.

No Joker. No obligatory Joker cameo. Gotham has more than one fucking villain.

And here's the hook: Wesker gets hold of Bruce's private contingency files about his own family.

Every vulnerability. Every fear. Every possibility Bruce once imagined in case one of his protégés became a threat.

He weaponizes those files, revealing them to the people Bruce claims to trust.

And the family discovers something much worse than the villain's plan.

**Bruce really did write them.**

## The story

<text color="secondary" weight="medium" size="xs">Three acts. One spectacularly dysfunctional family.</text>

### Act I — The Bat

We open with Batman destroying a gang's operations in an abandoned Gotham shipping terminal.

Ritchson's Bruce is terrifying. No quips during the fight. No unnecessary theatrics. He moves with the efficiency of a man who knows exactly what a human body can and cannot withstand.

Afterward, one of the arrested criminals looks up at him.

“You're fucking enormous.”

Batman looks down.

“Observant.”

Back at the Batcave, Alfred is waiting with dinner.

Six place settings.

Bruce stares at them.

“Why are there six plates?”

“Because, Master Bruce, at some point I intend for this house to contain people who are alive.”

And there it is. The movie's actual conflict.

Dick hasn't been home in months. Barbara answers operational calls but ignores Bruce's personal messages. Jason refuses to speak to him. Tim is increasingly tired of being treated like a junior employee.

Cassandra is the only one who regularly comes by, mostly because Alfred feeds her.

Then the contingency files begin arriving.

### Act II — The Family

Wesker orchestrates a citywide criminal operation using those files to draw the family apart. He expects them to react independently, emotionally, and predictably.

The plan works.

Dick learns Bruce had documented scenarios in which Nightwing might betray him.

Barbara discovers that Bruce kept contingencies for disabling Oracle's systems.

Jason finds a file treating him as an unacceptable recurrence risk.

The family fractures.

Bruce insists that the files were precautions.

**Nobody accepts that explanation.**

Barbara finally says what everybody has been thinking:

“Bruce, you made plans for every possible way we could hurt you. Did you ever consider making a plan for how you could stop hurting us?”

Silence.

That's the scene Mike Flanagan gets to direct. No music. No camera trick. No explosion to rescue Bruce from answering.

### Act III — The Family Business

Wesker takes control of a Gotham charity event attended by hundreds of children and their families, intending to force Batman into an impossible public choice.

Bruce's first instinct is to go alone.

Dick stops him.

“You don't get to make that decision for all of us anymore.”

And Bruce finally does something he has never been good at.

He asks for help.

Not as Batman issuing orders.

As Bruce Wayne asking his family.

The finale isn't about Batman overpowering Scarface.

It's about Bruce giving up control.

Dick leads the physical rescue. Barbara owns the intelligence operation. Tim identifies the central weakness in Wesker's network. Cassandra dismantles his inner security. Jason prevents civilians from being caught in the crossfire.

Bruce takes the most dangerous position, not because he believes he must do everything himself, but because that's where his strength is genuinely needed.

The villain loses because he expected one man surrounded by subordinates.

**He encounters a family of independent heroes who choose to work together.**

## The dinner scene

This is the scene I absolutely refuse to let Gunn turn into a throwaway joke.

Wayne Manor. Two weeks after the crisis.

Dick has come to dinner.

Barbara is there. So is Tim. Cassandra is eating like she hasn't seen food in three days.

Jason hasn't arrived.

Bruce sits at the table in a sweater. No tactical equipment. No screens.

He's visibly uncomfortable.

Alfred serves dinner.

Dick breaks the silence.

> **DICK:** You know, you could have just called.
>
> **BRUCE:** I did call.
>
> **BARBARA:** You sent encrypted messages marked urgent.
>
> **BRUCE:** They were urgent.
>
> **BARBARA:** One of them was about Thanksgiving.
>
> **TIM:** To be fair, Alfred's Thanksgiving is serious business.
>
> **ALFRED:** Thank you, Master Timothy.
>
> **DICK:** Bruce. You don't have to manufacture an emergency to get us in the same room.
>
> **BRUCE:** I know.
>
> **BARBARA:** Do you?
>
> **BRUCE:** I'm trying to.

The room gets quiet.

Bruce looks at Dick.

> **BRUCE:** I thought if I prepared for everything, I could keep you safe.
>
> **DICK:** You couldn't.
>
> **BRUCE:** No.
>
> **DICK:** And you couldn't make us stay.
>
> **BRUCE:** No.
>
> **DICK:** So what happens now?
>
> **BRUCE:** I ask whether you'd like to come back next Sunday.

Dick looks at Barbara.

Barbara considers Bruce for a moment.

> **BARBARA:** Are you going to interrogate everybody about what they've been doing all week?
>
> **BRUCE:** Probably.
>
> **BARBARA:** At least he's being honest.
>
> **ALFRED:** Progress, Miss Gordon. At last.

Then the front door opens.

Jason walks in.

He looks at the table. The empty seat. Bruce.

> **JASON:** I'm not staying.
>
> **ALFRED:** Of course not, sir. Shall I serve your dinner in a takeaway container?
>
> **JASON:** What's for dinner?
>
> **ALFRED:** Roast beef.
>
> **JASON:** ...Fuck.

And Jason sits down.

Nobody cheers.

Bruce doesn't rush over to hug him.

Alfred simply puts another plate on the table.

**That's the emotional victory.**

Not reconciliation completed. Reconciliation finally beginning.

## The Gunn touch

The last shot is not Batman on a rooftop.

It's Wayne Manor after dinner.

Dick and Jason arguing in the kitchen. Barbara and Tim arguing about security software. Cassandra feeding something she's not supposed to feed to the dog.

Alfred washing dishes.

Bruce standing in the doorway, watching his family make an absolute mess of his house.

He smiles.

Alfred notices.

“Something amusing, Master Bruce?”

“No.”

A crash comes from the kitchen.

Jason shouts, “DICK, YOU ASSHOLE!”

Bruce closes his eyes.

“Maybe.”

**Cut to black.**

End credits: *This Must Be the Place* by Talking Heads.

That's the Bat-Family movie I want.
